claims.text: Alloy composition governs whether a stable protective oxide forms and persists above 900 °C.
The oxide layer's crystal structure governs its stability and persistence.
The oxide layer's thickness governs its stability and persistence.
Adherence of the oxide layer to the alloy substrate governs its stability and persistence.
Composition influences oxide-layer formation and stability.
CrFeCoNiSi may form a more stable and adherent oxide layer than CrFeCoNiMn or CrFeCoNiAl.
Under the proposed exposure, a stable and coherent protective oxide layer will form and persist.
The protective oxide layer will grow slowly.
The protective oxide layer will exhibit minimal cracking and spallation.
Some CrFeCoNiX alloys have unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation.
The hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys initially in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
The proposed exposure is an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere above 900 °C.
The hypothesis excludes temperatures below 900 °C, non-oxidative or non-corrosive atmospheres, and compositions outside the CrFeCoNiX family.
Grain size and impurities may affect oxide-layer stability.
Cracking, spallation, or significant alloy degradation within 100 hours above 900 °C is designated as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits 'minimal' cracking or spallation, whereas the falsification rule treats any cracking or spallation as falsifying, leaving the acceptable failure threshold inconsistent.
